title.text: A few laws drivers should know

lines.text: The manual's law list is short

narration.text: This section of the manual covers a handful of state laws that matter to drivers, and it says plainly that it does not address every law. Treat it as a useful starting point rather than the complete body of South Carolina traffic law. The first law it covers connects your license application to the federal Selective Service. Young male applicants complete an extra form, and their information is shared automatically at a certain age. In this unit you will learn who fills out the form, what is sent, when it is sent and the one exception.

lines.text: Male citizens and immigrants under twenty-six
Permit, license or ID card applications

narration.text: Male United States citizens and immigrants younger than twenty-six must complete form four-forty-seven-SEL, the Supplement for South Carolina Credential Selective Service Requirements, when they apply for a permit, a license or an identification card. The rule covers all three credentials alike, so a young man applying only for an identification card still completes the form. It is simply part of the application packet for most young male applicants, and having it filled out ahead of time keeps the branch visit moving smoothly. Keep the form age and the transfer age clearly separate.

lines.text: Sent when the applicant turns eighteen
Name, address, birth date, sex, SSN, date

narration.text: When such an applicant turns eighteen, the SCDMV must send his name, address, date of birth, sex, Social Security number and application date to the United States Selective Service, as state law requires. This is an automatic transfer tied to the credential, so the applicant does not have to file anything else. The one exception the manual names is physical surrender: the transfer does not happen if the applicant physically surrenders the permit, license or identification card before turning eighteen. Without that surrender, the data goes on schedule.

Here is the trap. Two different ages appear in this rule, and they are easy to swap. The form is required for male applicants under twenty-six, while the SCDMV only sends the data to the Selective Service once the applicant reaches eighteen. So a sixteen-year-old completes the form now, but nothing is sent until his eighteenth birthday, and a twenty-two-year-old completes the form and his data can be sent right away because he is already past eighteen. Keep the form age and the transfer age in separate boxes. Keep the form age and the transfer age clearly separate.

Here is a quick check: a young male applicant completed the Selective Service form when he got his permit at fifteen. What is the one thing that would stop the SCDMV from sending his data when he turns eighteen? The answer is physically surrendering the permit, license or identification card before his eighteenth birthday. That is the only exception the manual names. Otherwise, the SCDMV must send his name, address, date of birth, sex, Social Security number and application date to the Selective Service once he turns eighteen. Keep the form age and the transfer age clearly separate.

To close, this part of the manual covers only a few laws of interest to drivers and does not address every law. Male citizens and immigrants younger than twenty-six complete form four-forty-seven-SEL when applying for a permit, license or identification card. When the applicant turns eighteen, the SCDMV sends his personal details to the Selective Service, unless he physically surrenders the credential before that birthday. Remember the two ages: twenty-six for the form, eighteen for the transfer. Keep the form age and the transfer age clearly separate.

Minors can register, but the final decision belongs to a parent or guardian.

prompt.text: What mark appears on a license when the holder registers as a donor?

lines.text: Offered at every issuance and renewal

narration.text: Each time you apply for or renew a license, beginner's permit or identification card in South Carolina, you can register as an organ and tissue donor. This unit explains what registering does, how it shows on your card, why it is more than a simple preference, who makes the final decision for younger registrants, and how to change your decision later. Understanding these points lets you make an informed choice at the counter rather than guessing about what the checkbox really means for you and your family. The choice is yours to make at the counter.

You can register as an organ and tissue donor when you apply for or renew a license, permit or identification card. Registering adds your identity information to the South Carolina Donor Registry and puts a red heart on your license, permit or card. The red heart is the visible donor marker that an officer or medic would see. Choosing to be a donor is a legally binding agreement under the South Carolina Uniform Anatomical Gift Act, so the decision carries real legal weight rather than being a simple note of preference. The choice is yours to make at the counter.

title.text: Binding, but not final for minors

narration.text: Here is a point that confuses many families. Registering as a donor is a legally binding agreement, yet for a registrant under eighteen, the parent or legal guardian makes the final decision about donation. So a teen's registration still counts and is recorded, but it is not final on its own. Both statements are true at once. The binding agreement applies to the registration itself, and the law adds a safeguard for minors by leaving the final word with a parent or guardian until the registrant reaches eighteen. The choice is yours to make at the counter.

lines.text: Use the Donate Life SC website

narration.text: If you want to change or update your donor decision, you use the Donate Life South Carolina website, as state law sets out. The change goes through the registry website rather than a branch office. That means you can revisit your choice at any time without waiting for your next license renewal. If you registered as a teen and your views change as an adult, the website is where you update the registry. Knowing this makes the decision at the counter feel less permanent, while it still remains a legally binding agreement until you change it.

Here is a quick check: a driver chooses to register as an organ and tissue donor while renewing a license. What mark will appear on the new license? The answer is a red heart. Registering adds the driver's identity information to the South Carolina Donor Registry and puts a red heart on the license, permit or identification card. That heart is the visible donor marker that officers and medics can see. If the driver later changes their mind, the Donate Life South Carolina website is where the decision is updated. The choice is yours to make at the counter.

lines.text: Parent or guardian has the final say

narration.text: Teens are offered the same choice as adults when they apply for a permit or license. If you register as a donor before turning eighteen, your parent or legal guardian makes the final decision about donation. Talking with family about the choice at the time of registration helps everyone understand your wishes. The registration still adds you to the registry and puts the red heart on your card, so the decision is recorded and visible, while the final say for a minor rests with a parent or guardian under the law. The choice is yours to make at the counter.

To close, you can register as an organ and tissue donor whenever you apply for or renew a license, beginner's permit or identification card. Registering adds you to the South Carolina Donor Registry and puts a red heart on your card. The choice is a legally binding agreement under the state's anatomical gift law, though for registrants under eighteen a parent or legal guardian makes the final decision. To change or update your choice, use the Donate Life South Carolina website rather than visiting a branch. The choice is yours to make at the counter.

Simple in-car habits prevent littering in the first place.

prompt.text: What extra penalty can a court add for littering beyond a fine?

answer.text: Pick up roadside litter under court supervision.

narration.text: South Carolina treats roadside littering as a serious matter. Throwing trash along streets and highways is illegal, and the penalties go beyond a scolding. In this unit you will learn what can happen to a litter offender, why cigarette butts count as litter, and the simple habit the manual suggests for keeping trash inside the vehicle until it reaches a proper trash can. These rules protect the roads you drive every day, and following them is easy once a container in the car becomes part of your routine. Every piece of trash belongs in a container, never on the road.

Throwing trash along streets and highways is illegal, and offenders can be arrested and fined. A court may also order a litter offender to pick up roadside litter under court supervision, on top of a fine. So a litter offender can face both a fine and a court order to clean up the roadside. That makes littering a criminal matter rather than a simple courtesy issue. The cost of tossing one item out of a window can add up to a fine, an arrest record and hours of supervised cleanup work along the road. Every piece of trash belongs in a container, never on the road.

A common myth is that a cigarette butt flicked out of a window is too small to count. It is not. Cigarettes and cigarette butts count as litter and should stay inside the vehicle until they can be thrown away properly. Flicking a butt out of the window is littering, with the same possible arrest, fine and court-ordered cleanup as any other trash. If you smoke, keep a container for butts in the vehicle and empty it into a trash can, just as you would with cups or wrappers. Every piece of trash belongs in a container, never on the road.

Empty it when it is full

narration.text: The manual suggests keeping a litter container in the vehicle and emptying it into a trash can once it is full. Paper cups, candy wrappers and bottles are its examples of the kind of litter to collect there. The container gives every piece of trash a place to go, so nothing ends up on the floor or out the window. It is a small habit that prevents roadside litter and the penalties that come with it. Empty the container at home or at a gas station whenever it fills up. Every piece of trash belongs in a container, never on the road. A clean habit protects both the roads and your record.

The answer is pick up roadside litter under court supervision. A litter offender can face both a fine and a court order for supervised cleanup, and offenders can also be arrested. Remember that cigarette butts count as litter too, so the same penalties apply to a butt flicked out of a window as to a bag of trash left on the shoulder. Every piece of trash belongs in a container, never on the road. A clean habit protects both the roads and your record.

lines.text: Keep a container in the car

narration.text: To close, throwing trash along streets and highways is illegal, and offenders can be arrested and fined, with a court able to add supervised roadside cleanup on top of the fine. Cigarettes and cigarette butts count as litter and should stay in the vehicle until you can throw them away properly. The manual's simple fix is a litter container in the vehicle for things like paper cups, candy wrappers and bottles, emptied into a trash can whenever it is full. That habit keeps both the roads and your record clean. Every piece of trash belongs in a container, never on the road.

why_how.text: Golf carts on public roads follow specific age, license, distance and road rules.
Some vehicles are covered by separate SCDMV manuals.

scenario.text: Nora, sixteen with a valid driver's license, wants to drive her family's registered golf cart to a friend's house.

reasoning.text: By day, the cart may go within four miles of its registered address, and near a gated community only on secondary roads posted at thirty-five miles per hour or less.

result.text: The friend lives three miles away along a road posted at thirty, so Nora may make the daytime trip.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking any sixteen-year-old may drive a golf cart.

correction.text: A golf cart driver must be at least sixteen and also hold a valid driver's license.

memory_support.text: Sixteen and licensed, decal on, four miles by day, thirty-five or slower roads.

prompt.text: How far from the registered address may a golf cart be driven in the daytime?

rationale.text: Daytime golf cart driving is allowed within four miles of the address on the registration certificate.

narration.text: Golf carts are a common sight in some South Carolina communities, and when they use public roads they follow specific rules. In this unit you will learn who may drive a golf cart, what the cart must display, how far it may travel by day, which roads it may use, and where the manual sends you for rules about commercial vehicles, mopeds, motorcycles and large recreational vehicles. These details matter for families who use carts for short trips, because a cart on the wrong road or too far from home breaks the law. Check the driver, the cart and the road before every trip.

Driving a golf cart requires being at least sixteen with a valid driver's license, and the cart must carry an SCDMV-issued permit or registration decal. Golf carts are treated as licensed vehicles on public roads in South Carolina. The age and the license go together: a sixteen-year-old without a valid driver's license may not drive a golf cart on a public road, and a cart without its permit or decal should not be there either. Check both the driver and the cart before any trip leaves private property. Check the driver, the cart and the road before every trip.

lines.text: A valid license is required too

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because the golf cart rule mentions age sixteen, some families assume any sixteen-year-old can drive one. That is not true. The minimum age of sixteen also requires a valid driver's license, so age alone is not enough. A teen who has turned sixteen but has only a beginner's permit, or no license at all, may not drive a golf cart on a public road. Before handing over the keys, confirm that the driver is at least sixteen and holds a valid driver's license, and that the cart has its decal. Check the driver, the cart and the road before every trip.

title.text: How far and on which roads

lines.text: Four miles from the registered address
Or four miles from a community gate

narration.text: Daytime golf cart driving is allowed within four miles of the address on the cart's registration certificate. A golf cart may also be driven by day within four miles of a gated community's gate, so the gate can serve as the starting point for the four-mile limit. Either way, golf carts are limited to secondary streets and highways posted at thirty-five miles per hour or less, as state law sets out. Any road posted faster than thirty-five miles per hour is off limits, even if it lies inside the four-mile area. Check the driver, the cart and the road before every trip.

lines.text: How far from the registered address?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a licensed driver plans a daytime golf cart trip starting from the cart's registered address. How far from that address may the cart travel? The answer is within four miles. Daytime golf cart driving is allowed within four miles of the address on the cart's registration certificate, or within four miles of a gated community's gate. And no matter how short the trip, the cart must stay on secondary streets and highways posted at thirty-five miles per hour or less. Check the driver, the cart and the road before every trip.

lines.text: Mopeds and motorcycles: their own manual

narration.text: This manual does not cover every type of vehicle. For commercial motor vehicles, it sends readers to the SCDMV Commercial Driver's License Manual. Mopeds and motorcycles are covered in the SCDMV Motorcycle and Moped Operator's Manual, and large non-commercial and recreational vehicles are covered in the Large Non-Commercial and Recreational Vehicles Driver's Manual. So mopeds share a manual with motorcycles, while large non-commercial vehicles share one with recreational vehicles. If you drive one of these, pick up the right manual too.

To close, a golf cart driver must be at least sixteen and hold a valid driver's license, and the cart must carry an SCDMV permit or registration decal. By day, the cart may travel within four miles of its registered address or of a gated community's gate, but only on secondary streets and highways posted at thirty-five miles per hour or less. For commercial vehicles, mopeds and motorcycles, and large non-commercial or recreational vehicles, the SCDMV publishes separate manuals that cover their rules. Check the driver, the cart and the road before every trip.
